abstract: APOE encodes the principal lipid-transporting protein in the brain, and lipid dysregulation is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. The APOE4 allele, together with advanced age and female sex, are major risk factors for late-onset AD. Yet how these risk factors interact to reshape lipid composition and transport in the brain remains unclear. Herein, we characterize lipidomic profiles in the brain, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood of individuals with or without AD, as well as of mice expressing humanized APOE. We identify brain lipidomic shifts associated with AD in humans, including relative depletion of highly unsaturated lipids, with many changes resembling those associated with APOE4 alone. Individuals with AD show striking depletion of lipoprotein particle (LP)-associated lipid abundance in the CSF. Additionally, humanized APOE4 mice exhibit an age-dependent deficit in CSF LP-associated lipid abundance relative to APOE3 mice. Accordingly, we leverage these insights to engineer brain-inspired reconstituted LPs (rLPs) with the goal of restoring lipid transport in the brain. rLPs promote cholesterol efflux from human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived APOE4 astrocytes in vitro. In an AD mouse model (5xFAD) expressing humanized APOE4, these nanoparticles reduce lipid-droplet accumulation, facilitate amyloid-beta clearance, enhance synaptic integrity, and improve cognitive function. Together, our results provide a resource mapping lipidomic changes across the Alzheimer's risk triad and demonstrate that engineered rLPs can counter lipid accumulation and associated pathology in the brain, and cognitive deficits in vivo.
